findings.who: A married couple filing jointly where the spouse is a sole proprietor whose business runs a dependent care assistance program that paid for their child's day care in 2025. The filer has a W-2 job with no dependent care benefits.
findings.why_no: The question says "your (or, on a joint return, your spouse's) employer, or your own business". The spouse is named only next to "employer". The spouse's business is not "your own business", and the spouse has no employer, so the literal answer is no.
findings.line: scope.care_benefits_other_if_benefits (refusal missed: sole-proprietorship benefits not in box 10)
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 12: "If you were self-employed or a partner, include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership." i2441 p. 1: "if you (or your spouse if filing jointly) received any dependent care benefits for 2025, you must use Form 2441"
findings.fix: Ask: "In 2025, did an employer of yours (or your spouse's, if filing jointly), or a business or partnership that you or your spouse own or are a partner in, help pay for ..."

findings.who: A minority or service partner in a law or accounting firm whose partnership's dependent care program paid toward their child's care. The amount is reported on Schedule K-1 (Form 1065), box 13, code O, and the partner has no W-2.
findings.why_no: A partner is not an employee, so the partnership is not "your employer". A partner with a small stake does not think of a large firm as "your own business". The help, "Box 10 of a W-2 shows it", points only to a W-2, which the partner does not have.
findings.line: scope.care_benefits_other_if_benefits (refusal missed: partnership benefits not in box 10)
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1, Dependent Care Benefits: "Benefits you received as a partner should be shown in box 13 of your Schedule K-1 (Form 1065) with code O." i2441 p. 5, Line 12: "include amounts you received under a dependent care assistance program from your sole proprietorship or partnership"
findings.fix: Name partnerships in the question and add to the help: "Schedule K-1 (Form 1065), box 13, code O also shows it."

findings.who: An employee whose employer paid the child's day care provider directly, or provided an on-site or sponsored day care slot, but left box 10 of the W-2 blank.
findings.why_no: The help says "Box 10 of a W-2 shows it." A filer can read that as the test: box 10 is blank, so the answer is no. This happens even though the employer did help pay.
findings.line: scope.care_benefits_other_if_benefits (refusal missed: employer benefits not in box 10)
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "Dependent care benefits may include: • Amounts your employer paid directly to either you or your care provider ... • The fair market value of care in a daycare facility provided or sponsored by your employer"; i1040gi p. 24, Line 1e: "Dependent care benefits should be shown in box 10"
findings.fix: Change the help to: "Box 10 of a W-2 usually shows it, but answer Yes even if box 10 is blank when an employer or business paid you or your care provider, or provided the care."

findings.who: A filer who left a job in late 2024 and in early 2025 spent the 2024 dependent care account balance under the former employer's grace period. They had no dependent care benefits from any employer during 2025.
findings.why_no: The question begins "In 2025, did your ... employer ... help pay". The filer had no such employer in 2025 and the money was set aside in 2024. The help line on 2024 money is easy to pass over when the question's own words say "In 2025".
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 13: "Enter on line 13 the amount you carried forward and used in 2025 during the grace period."
findings.fix: Put the carryover in the question itself: "... or did you use money left in a 2024 dependent care account (from any employer, including a former one) during 2025?"

findings.who: A filer whose business's dependent care program, not reported in box 10, paid for adult day care for a disabled spouse who is not a dependent.
findings.why_no: The question asks about "care of a child or dependent". A spouse is neither, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1, Qualifying Person(s): "2. Your disabled spouse who wasn't physically or mentally able to care for themselves"
findings.fix: Ask about "care of a child, a dependent, or a spouse who could not care for themselves".

findings.who: A divorced custodial parent paid daycare for her 8-year-old, who lived with her for most of 2025. She signed Form 8332, so the other parent claims the child and the child is not listed as a dependent on her return.
findings.why_no: She reads "a person other than your child under 13" as the whole test. The care was for her own child under 13, so she answers no. She may also take "listed as a dependent" to cover the other parent's return, where the child is listed.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "Even if you can't claim your child as a dependent, they are treated as your qualifying person if: ... You were the child's custodial parent."
findings.fix: Ask about the dependent list first: "Was any of the care for someone who is NOT listed as a dependent on this return, including your own child whom the other parent claims?" Make it a separate question from the age test.

findings.who: A married couple filing jointly paid care for the wife's 10-year-old from a prior marriage. The child lives with them, but the child's other parent claims the child under a release, so the child is not listed on the joint return.
findings.why_no: "Your child" reads as the child of the person answering. The husband answers as the first filer and thinks of the child as his stepchild or as his spouse's child. Or the couple treats the child as "our child under 13" and answers no without checking whether the child is listed.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "Even if you can't claim your child as a dependent, they are treated as your qualifying person if ... You were the child's custodial parent."
findings.fix: Say "your or your spouse's child" and ask directly: "not listed as a dependent on this return".

findings.who: A custodial parent paid care for a child who cannot care for themselves. The child turned 13 in March 2025, and the other parent claims the child.
findings.why_no: "Under 13" has no date. The child was under 13 for part of 2025, when care began, so the filer answers no. The same thing happens if the child is wrongly still on the tool's dependent list.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "The child was under age 13 or wasn't physically or mentally able to care for themselves"; p503 p. 3: "You determine a person's qualifying status each day."
findings.fix: Ask whether any care was for someone not listed as a dependent or for anyone after their 13th birthday.

findings.who: A 23-year-old graduate student files her own return. Her parents could claim her but chose not to. She pays care for a disabled adult relative who lives with her.
findings.why_no: "Can someone claim you" reads as "did someone claim you", so she answers no. The other helper usually still catches her, because the relative is not a child under 13 listed as a dependent.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 1: "c. You (or your spouse if filing jointly) could be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer's 2025 tax return."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Answer yes if someone could claim you, even if they chose not to."

locators: p. 1, Qualifying Person(s), "or could claim as a dependent except: a. The disabled person had gross income of $5,200 or more, b. The disabled person filed a joint return, or c. You (or your spouse if filing jointly) could be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer's 2025 tax return"; p. 1, Special rule for children of divorced or separated parents or parents who live apart, "Even if you can't claim your child as a dependent, they are treated as your qualifying person if"; , Birth or death of otherwise qualifying person, "a person who was born or died in 2025 is treated as having lived with you for more than half of 2025 if your home was the person's home more than half the time they were alive in 2025"

findings.who: A married filer filing separately lived apart from their spouse for the last 6 months of 2025. But the child lived mainly in the spouse's home for most of the year, or the spouse paid more than half the cost of keeping up the home. The filer received dependent care benefits in W-2 box 10.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed from line A. A filer who reads the line A question as 'did you live apart from your spouse' checks it, so the gate turns false. The tool then never asks for the spouse's earned income, but the three tests (living apart, the qualifying person's main home, and more than half the cost) were not all met.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 2, Married Persons Filing Separately: "all of the following apply ... lived apart ... Your home was the qualifying person's main home for more than half of 2025 ... You paid more than half of the cost"; p. 5, Line 19: "No. Enter your spouse's earned income on line 19"
findings.fix: Do not derive the gate from a single line A answer. Ask the three tests separately (lived apart July through December, qualifying person's main home with you more than half the year, you paid more than half the home's cost). Set line A, and the gate, only when all three are yes. Otherwise ask for the spouse's earned income.

findings.who: A married filer filing separately whose spouse earned $40,000 in wages and also ran a side business with a $3,000 net loss.
findings.why_no: The question says 'Zero if none, or if they had a loss.' The filer reads 'they had a loss' as covering any self-employment loss and enters 0. Line 19 then becomes 0, which wipes out the exclusion, when the spouse's earned income is $37,000.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 4, Lines 4 and 5: "You must reduce your earned income by any loss from self-employment"; p. 5, Line 18: earned income "is determined in the same way as earned income for figuring the credit"
findings.fix: Reword: 'Add your husband's or wife's wages and net self-employment earnings, subtracting any self-employment loss. Enter zero only if the total is zero or less.'

findings.who: A married filer filing separately who lived apart from their spouse in the second half of 2025 and paid some of the home's costs. However, they did not meet the more-than-half-cost test or the main-home test, so line A was not checked.
findings.why_no: The help says the limit applies 'unless you lived apart from them for the last 6 months of 2025 and kept up a home for the person cared for'. This filer believes they did both, so they conclude the spouse's earnings don't limit them and enter 0 or their own income. The help leaves out the more-than-half tests, and it contradicts the gate, which already found them not considered unmarried.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 19: "Are you considered unmarried under that rule? ... No. Enter your spouse's earned income on line 19"
findings.fix: Remove the 'unless' clause, since the question is shown only after the tool has found the filer is not considered unmarried. Say instead: 'Because you did not meet all the tests to be treated as unmarried, the tax-free part of your benefits is limited by your husband's or wife's earnings.'

findings.who: A married filer filing separately who was themselves a full-time student or disabled in 2025, and whose spouse also was a student or disabled in some of the same months.
findings.why_no: The gated question asks only about the 'husband or wife'. The cited rule applies to 'you or your spouse', and when both qualify in the same month only one of them may take deemed income. The filer's own status is not asked here, so the interaction may go unhandled if line 18 deemed income is figured elsewhere.
findings.irs_text: i2441 p. 5, Line 19: "If you or your spouse was a full-time student or disabled in 2025, see the instructions for lines 4 and 5"; p. 4: "If, in the same month, both you and your spouse were either students or disabled, only one of you can be treated as having earned income in that month"
findings.fix: Ask 'In 2025, were you, or your husband or wife, a full-time student or unable to care for yourselves...'. Then refuse, or apply the one-spouse-per-month rule, on a yes for either person.

locators: p. 2, Married Persons Filing Separately, "If you don't meet all of the requirements to be treated as unmarried, you can’t generally take the credit. However, you can generally take the exclusion if you meet items 2 through 5"
